chapters.title: Strange Fire
chapters.html:
Leviticus 10

Strange Fire

1Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu each took his fire pan, put fire in it, laid incense on it, and offered before the LORD strange fire, which He had not commanded them.

2Fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them, and they died before the LORD.

3Moses said to Aaron, "This is what the LORD spoke of when He said: Through those near Me I will be shown holy, and before all the people I will be honored." Aaron was silent.

4Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel, Aaron's uncle, and said to them, "Come near, carry your brothers away from the front of the holy place, outside the camp."

5They came near and carried them in their tunics outside the camp, as Moses had said.

6Moses said to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar his sons, "Do not let your hair hang loose and do not tear your clothes, or you will die and anger will come on the whole congregation. But your brothers, the whole house of Israel, may weep for those the LORD has burned.

7Do not go out from the entrance of the tent of meeting, or you will die, because the LORD's anointing oil is on you." They did as Moses said.

What the Priests May Not Do

8The LORD spoke to Aaron, saying,

9"Do not drink wine or strong drink, you or your sons with you, when you come into the tent of meeting, or you will die. It is a lasting statute through your generations,

10and so that you can separate the holy from the ordinary, and the unclean from the clean,

11and teach the sons of Israel all the statutes the LORD has spoken to them through Moses."

The Meal That Was Not Eaten

12Moses spoke to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar, his remaining sons: "Take the grain offering that is left from the LORD's offerings by fire and eat it unleavened beside the altar, because it is most holy.

13You shall eat it in a holy place, because it is your due and your sons' due from the LORD's offerings by fire; for so I was commanded.

14You shall eat the breast that was waved and the thigh that was lifted off in a clean place — you and your sons and your daughters with you — because they are given as your due and your sons' due from the peace offerings of the sons of Israel.

15They shall bring the thigh that is lifted off and the breast that is waved, together with the fat pieces for the offerings by fire, to wave them before the LORD; and it shall be yours and your sons' with you as a lasting due, as the LORD has commanded."

16Moses searched and searched for the goat of the sin offering, and here — it had been burned. He was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron's remaining sons, and said,

17"Why did you not eat the sin offering in the holy place? It is most holy, and He gave it to you to carry the guilt of the congregation, to make atonement for them before the LORD.

18Look — its blood was not brought inside the holy place. You should certainly have eaten it in the holy place, as I commanded."

19Aaron said to Moses, "Look — today they brought their sin offering and their burnt offering before the LORD, and things like this have happened to me. If I had eaten a sin offering today, would that have been good in the eyes of the LORD?"

20Moses heard, and it was good in his eyes.

Notes

  • v1 "strange fire" — esh zarah, and the adjective is already on the books. Exodus 30:9 forbids qetoret zarah, strange incense, on the incense altar, in a verse about equipment written before either man was ordained. What the text never supplies is what made it strange. The only reason given is negative: which He had not commanded them. Not that it was forbidden — that it was not ordered. In a book where every action so far has been prescribed down to which finger, doing something unprescribed turns out to be the offense.

  • vv1, 3, 4 the word that runs through the chapter — qarav, to come near, is the verb behind every offering in chapters 1 through 9: an offering is a qorban, a thing brought near. Here Nadab and Abihu bring near strange fire (v1); Moses says God will be shown holy bi-qrovai, through those near Me (v3); and the cousins who carry the bodies out are told qirvu, come near (v4). The same root covers the offering, the offenders, and the men who clear away what is left.

  • v3 the quotation with no source — Moses says this is what the LORD spoke, and then quotes a sentence that is recorded nowhere in the Torah. The nearest thing to it is Exodus 29:43, and it shall be made holy by My glory — said of the tent, not of people. The verb here, eqqadesh, I will be shown holy, occurs in this form once in the Hebrew Bible, in this verse. Aaron has just lost two sons, and the explanation he is given is a quotation the reader has never been shown.

  • v3 "Aaron was silent" — va-yiddom Aharon, two words, and it ends the scene. This exact form occurs four times in the Bible, and one of the others is Joshua 10:13, and the sun stood still. The verb is not only about sound; it is about a thing stopping. What Aaron does is not described as grief, acceptance, shock, or protest. He simply comes to a halt, and the text moves on to the disposal of the bodies.

  • v5 "carried them in their tunics" — the garments Moses put on them in 8:13. Whether the tunics are what the bodies were carried in or carried by is not settled by the Hebrew, but either way, the last mention of Nadab and Abihu in the chapter is their priestly clothing, intact. The fire consumed the men and not the uniform.

  • v6 "do not let your hair hang loose" — al tifra'u, from para, to unbind or let run wild, and with do not tear your clothes it names the two standard gestures of mourning. Aaron and his two surviving sons are forbidden both, and forbidden to leave the doorway (v7). Their brothers may be wept for by the entire nation — the text says so in the same breath — by everyone except the three men who actually lost them.

  • v6 "anger will come" — yiqtsof, and the Hebrew gives the verb no subject at all: and upon the whole congregation it will be angry. Wrath is spoken of as a thing that arrives rather than as something somebody does. English cannot leave a verb unattached like that, and every translation has to decide whether to supply He. Nothing in the verse supplies it.

  • v9 wine, placed here — the ban on drinking before entering the tent arrives immediately after two priests die doing something unauthorized, and is addressed to Aaron directly — one of very few times in the Torah God speaks to him without Moses. The text does not say Nadab and Abihu had been drinking. It puts the law here, and says nothing.

  • v10 "separate the holy from the ordinary" — le-havdil, the verb of Genesis 1: God separated light from darkness, the waters from the waters, day from night. It is the work of the first three days, and it is handed here to the priesthood as its job description — holy from ordinary, unclean from clean. What God did to the world, the priest is to keep doing inside the camp.

  • v14 "and your daughters with you" — the breast and the thigh may be eaten by the priest's whole household, daughters included, because they are eaten in a clean place rather than a holy one. The distinction of v10 does immediate work: the most holy portions are restricted to males in the courtyard, and these are not most holy, so the family eats them at home.

  • v16 "searched and searched" — darosh darash, the verb doubled with itself, which is Hebrew leaning on a word. Darash is to seek, inquire, investigate — the verb behind midrash. Moses hunts for the goat, finds it burnt, and loses his temper at the two sons who are left, on the day their brothers died.

  • vv19–20 Aaron answers, and wins — his first words since the silence of v3, and he does not apologize. He points at the day itself: things like this have happened to me — the only phrase in the chapter that comes close to saying what he feels, and it does not name it. Then a question rather than a defense: would that have been good in the eyes of the LORD? And Moses, who has been right about everything since the first chapter, hears it and drops the charge. The book does not say who was correct about the law. It says the argument ended.

chapters.title: Clean and Unclean Creatures
chapters.html:
Leviticus 11

On the Land

1The LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them,

2"Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: These are the creatures you may eat out of all the animals on the earth.

3Among the animals, you may eat any that has a divided hoof, split in two, and brings up the cud.

4But you shall not eat these, among those that bring up the cud or have a divided hoof: the camel, because it brings up the cud but does not have a divided hoof — it is unclean for you;

5and the rock badger, because it brings up the cud but does not have a divided hoof — it is unclean for you;

6and the hare, because it brings up the cud but does not have a divided hoof — it is unclean for you;

7and the pig, because it has a divided hoof, split in two, but does not chew the cud — it is unclean for you.

8You shall not eat their flesh, and you shall not touch their carcasses. They are unclean for you.

In the Water

9Of all that lives in the water you may eat these: anything in the seas or the streams that has fins and scales.

10But anything in the seas and in the streams that does not have fins and scales, among all that swarms in the water and among all the living creatures in the water — they are loathsome to you.

11They shall be loathsome to you. You shall not eat their flesh, and you shall loathe their carcasses.

12Anything in the water that does not have fins and scales is loathsome to you.

The Birds

13Among the birds, these you shall loathe; they shall not be eaten, they are loathsome: the eagle, the bearded vulture, the black vulture,

14the kite and the falcon of every kind,

15every kind of raven,

16the ostrich, the nighthawk, the gull, and the hawk of every kind,

17the owl, the cormorant, the great owl,

18the white owl, the pelican, the carrion vulture,

19the stork, the heron of every kind, the hoopoe, and the bat.

Things That Swarm

20Every winged swarming thing that walks on all fours is loathsome to you.

21But among the winged swarming things that walk on all fours, you may eat those that have jointed legs above their feet for leaping on the ground.

22Of these you may eat: the locust of every kind, the bald locust of every kind, the cricket of every kind, and the grasshopper of every kind.

23But every other winged swarming thing that has four feet is loathsome to you.

What Touching Them Does

24By these you will become unclean. Anyone who touches their carcasses will be unclean until evening,

25and anyone who carries any of their carcasses shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening —

26every animal that has a divided hoof but not split in two, and does not bring up the cud. They are unclean for you; anyone who touches them will be unclean.

27Every creature that walks on its paws, among all the creatures that walk on all fours, is unclean for you. Anyone who touches their carcasses will be unclean until evening,

28and the one who carries their carcasses shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening. They are unclean for you.

29These are unclean for you among the things that swarm on the ground: the mole, the mouse, the great lizard of every kind,

30the gecko, the monitor lizard, the wall lizard, the skink, and the chameleon.

31These are the ones unclean for you among all the swarming things. Anyone who touches them when they are dead will be unclean until evening.

32Anything they fall on when they are dead becomes unclean — any article of wood, or clothing, or hide, or sackcloth — any article used for work. It shall be put in water and be unclean until evening, and then it is clean.

33If any of them falls into a clay pot, everything in it becomes unclean, and you shall break the pot.

34Any food that could be eaten, on which water has come, becomes unclean; and any drink that could be drunk, in any vessel, becomes unclean.

35Anything their carcass falls on becomes unclean. An oven or a stove shall be torn down. They are unclean, and unclean they shall be for you.

36But a spring or a cistern, a gathering of water, stays clean; and whoever touches their carcass in it becomes unclean.

37If any of their carcass falls on any seed that is to be sown, it is clean.

38But if water has been put on the seed and part of their carcass falls on it, it is unclean for you.

39If an animal that you may eat dies, whoever touches its carcass will be unclean until evening.

40Whoever eats from its carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening; and whoever carries its carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening.

Be Holy

41Everything that swarms on the ground is loathsome. It shall not be eaten.

42Whatever moves on its belly, whatever walks on all fours, whatever has many feet — anything that swarms on the ground — you shall not eat them, because they are loathsome.

43Do not make yourselves loathsome with anything that swarms, and do not make yourselves unclean by them, and so become unclean.

44Because I am the LORD your God. Set yourselves apart and be holy, because I am holy. Do not make yourselves unclean with any swarming thing that moves on the ground.

45Because I am the LORD who is bringing you up from the land of Egypt, to be your God. You shall be holy, because I am holy."

46This is the instruction for animals and birds and every living creature that moves in the water and every creature that swarms on the ground,

47to separate the unclean from the clean, and the creature that may be eaten from the creature that may not be eaten.

Notes

  • the chapter never says why — forty-seven verses of lists, and not one reason. Not health, not cruelty, not idolatry, not anything. The only thing resembling an explanation arrives at the very end and is about God rather than about the animals: be holy, because I am holy. Every reason an English reader has probably been given for these rules was supplied by somebody later; the text withholds all of them, and the withholding is deliberate enough to be a feature of the chapter.

  • v3 the two tests — a split hoof and chewing the cud, and an animal needs both. What makes the section memorable is that the four exceptions are argued out loud: camel, rock badger, hare, pig, each with its reason spelled out in the same sentence. The law is not content to list what is banned; it shows its working, and it is the only place in Leviticus that does.

  • v7 the pig — it gets one verse, the same shape as the camel's and the hare's, and not a syllable more. Of all the animals named here it is the one that became the emblem of the whole system, and the text treats it as the fourth item on a list of four. Whatever weight it later carried is not in these words.

  • vv13–19 the birds cannot all be identified — twenty names, and the English in every Bible is a best guess for most of them. Several occur only in this list and its twin at Deuteronomy 14, which gives a translator nothing to work with: a word used twice, in a list, with no description attached. Nesher may be the eagle or the griffon vulture; tachmas, shalakh, racham and dukhifat are essentially unknown. What survives clearly is the shape of the list — birds of prey, carrion birds, water birds — and one creature at the end that is not a bird at all.

  • vv18, 30 the same name in two lists — tinshemet appears in the bird list at v18 and again at v30 among the things that crawl on the ground. It occurs three times in the whole Hebrew Bible, twice in this chapter, in two different categories. English Bibles print two different animals for it, usually an owl and a chameleon, which is a solution rather than a reading. The text uses one word twice and does not remark on it.

  • v19 "and the bat" — the last entry in a list of birds. The text sorts creatures by how they move and where they live, not by anatomy; anything that flies belongs with flying things. The same logic runs through v20, where insects go on four although they have six legs, and v27, where what matters about an animal is that it walks on its paws.

  • vv10, 13, 41 "loathsome" — sheqets, and it is not the same word as tamei, unclean. Unclean is a condition, and it can be got rid of: wash, wait until evening, and it is over. Sheqets is a verdict, and the chapter also uses it as a verb — you shall loathe them (v11, 13) — which is the only thing in these forty-seven verses commanded as an attitude rather than an act.

  • v20 "walks on all fours" — insects have six legs. The phrase is not a mistake about anatomy, it is a category: walking on legs rather than standing upright, which is the same distinction v27 draws for animals that go on their paws and v42 draws for whatever goes on its belly. The chapter's categories are ways of moving.

  • v36 "a gathering of water" — miqveh mayim, and the phrase is out of Genesis 1:10: and the gathering of the waters He called seas. Here it names the one thing in the chapter that cannot be made unclean by contact. A pot is smashed, an oven is pulled down, a cistern is fine. The word later becomes the name of the ritual bath, mikveh, built on this verse.

  • v44 "be holy, because I am holy" — the first time this sentence appears in the Bible. Qadosh ani, I am holy, occurs five times in all, and every one of them is in Leviticus. It arrives at the end of a chapter about lizards and fins, and the logic is not that the creatures are evil but that Israel is being made to resemble somebody.

  • v45 "who is bringing you up" — ha-ma'aleh, a participle, not a past tense, and not the usual verb. The standard formula is I brought you out, hotseti, a finished act. Here it is ongoing and it is alah, to go up — the same verb Pharaoh feared at Exodus 1:10 and the one God used to Jacob at Genesis 46:4. The exodus is spoken of as still in progress while the people are standing at Sinai arguing about grasshoppers.

  • v47 "to separate the unclean from the clean" — le-havdil, closing the chapter with the verb it was handed in 10:10, which is the verb of the first three days of Genesis. The priest's job and the diet laws turn out to be the same job: keeping apart things that would otherwise run together.

By these you will become unclean. Anyone who touches their carcasses will be unclean until evening,
and anyone who carries any of their carcasses shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening —
every animal that has a divided hoof but not split in two, and does not bring up the cud. They are unclean for you; anyone who touches them will be unclean.
Every creature that walks on its paws, among all the creatures that walk on all fours, is unclean for you. Anyone who touches their carcasses will be unclean until evening,
and the one who carries their carcasses shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening. They are unclean for you.
These are unclean for you among the things that swarm on the ground: the mole, the mouse, the great lizard of every kind,
the gecko, the monitor lizard, the wall lizard, the skink, and the chameleon.
These are the ones unclean for you among all the swarming things. Anyone who touches them when they are dead will be unclean until evening.

Anything they fall on when they are dead becomes unclean — any article of wood, or clothing, or hide, or sackcloth — any article used for work. It shall be put in water and be unclean until evening, and then it is clean.
If any of them falls into a clay pot, everything in it becomes unclean, and you shall break the pot.
Any food that could be eaten, on which water has come, becomes unclean; and any drink that could be drunk, in any vessel, becomes unclean.
Anything their carcass falls on becomes unclean. An oven or a stove shall be torn down. They are unclean, and unclean they shall be for you.
But a spring or a cistern, a gathering of water, stays clean; and whoever touches their carcass in it becomes unclean.
If any of their carcass falls on any seed that is to be sown, it is clean.
But if water has been put on the seed and part of their carcass falls on it, it is unclean for you.
If an animal that you may eat dies, whoever touches its carcass will be unclean until evening.
Whoever eats from its carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening; and whoever carries its carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until evening.
Be Holy
Everything that swarms on the ground is loathsome. It shall not be eaten.
Whatever moves on its belly, whatever walks on all fours, whatever has many feet — anything that swarms on the ground — you shall not eat them, because they are loathsome.
Do not make yourselves loathsome with anything that swarms, and do not make yourselves unclean by them, and so become unclean.
Because I am the LORD your God. Set yourselves apart and be holy, because I am holy. Do not make yourselves unclean with any swarming thing that moves on the ground.
Because I am the LORD who is bringing you up from the land of Egypt, to be your God. You shall be holy, because I am holy."
This is the instruction for animals and birds and every living creature that moves in the water and every creature that swarms on the ground,
to separate the unclean from the clean, and the creature that may be eaten from the creature that may not be eaten.

chapters.title: After a Child Is Born
chapters.html:
Leviticus 12

After a Child Is Born

1The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,

2"Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: When a woman produces seed and bears a male, she shall be unclean seven days; she shall be unclean as in the days of her monthly separation.

3On the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.

4For thirty-three days she shall stay in the blood of her purifying. She shall not touch anything holy and shall not come into the sanctuary, until the days of her purifying are complete.

5If she bears a female, she shall be unclean two weeks, as in her separation; and for sixty-six days she shall stay in the blood of her purifying.

6When the days of her purifying are complete, for a son or for a daughter, she shall bring a year-old lamb for a burnt offering and a young pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering, to the entrance of the tent of meeting, to the priest.

7He shall present it before the LORD and make atonement for her, and she shall be clean from the flow of her blood. This is the instruction for the woman who gives birth, to a male or to a female.

8If she cannot afford a lamb, she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a burnt offering and one for a sin offering. The priest shall make atonement for her, and she shall be clean."

Notes

  • v2 "produces seed" — tazria, and the verb is the one used of plants. Genesis 1:12: vegetation yielding seed, esev mazria zera, the same stem. Hebrew has ordinary words for conceiving and for becoming pregnant, and the chapter opens with neither. It describes a woman bearing a child in the vocabulary of the third day of creation, and this is the only place in the Torah the verb is used of a person.

  • v3 one verse about the baby — circumcision on the eighth day is dropped into the middle of a law about the mother, in eight Hebrew words, with nothing before or after it. The chapter is not about the child; everything else in it concerns her days, her blood, her offering. The most consequential thing that happens to an Israelite boy gets a subordinate clause, because it is here only to mark where in her count it falls.

  • v4 "the blood of her purifying" — demei tohorah, and it is a strange pair of words. Blood is the substance that makes things unclean everywhere else in Leviticus; here the blood is the purifying. The phrase is not explained, and the situation it describes is neither uncleanness nor cleanness but a third state: she is not contagious any more — nothing here says anyone who touches her is affected — yet she cannot come near what is holy.

  • vv4–5 the count is doubled for a daughter — seven days and thirty-three for a son, fourteen and sixty-six for a daughter. Exactly twice, in both halves. The text gives no reason whatsoever, and none of the reasons later supplied is in the passage. What can be said is what the numbers do: nothing about the child changes, only the length of the mother's separation.

  • v6 a sin offering, for what — she brings a chatat, the offering of chapters 4 and 5, which is brought for a sin committed by mistake. No sin is named here, and nothing in the chapter says she did anything wrong. Whatever the chatat is doing in this law, it is not responding to an act — which is a warning about reading the word sin offering as though it always answered a sin.

  • v8 "if she cannot afford a lamb" — lo timtsa yadah, her hand does not find, next to 5:7's lo taggia yado, his hand does not reach. Two different idioms for the same thing in one book, and neither of them mentions money. The sliding scale works the same way it did in chapter 5: the cheaper offering is not a lesser rite, and the verse ends with the identical words the full version ends with — and she shall be clean.

  • v8 and the family in Luke 2 — the Greek of Luke 2:24 quotes this verse: a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. Three verses of that chapter are this law being carried out — circumcision on the eighth day (2:21), the days of purification (2:22), and then the offering, which is the substitute of v8 rather than the lamb of v6. Luke does not comment on which one they brought, and does not need to; anyone who knew this chapter could see it.

chapters.title: The Mark on the Skin
chapters.html:
Leviticus 13

What the Priest Looks For

1The LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying,

2"When a person has a swelling or a scab or a bright spot on the skin of his body, and it becomes a mark of blight on his skin, he shall be brought to Aaron the priest, or to one of his sons the priests.

3The priest shall look at the mark on the skin of the body. If the hair in the mark has turned white, and the mark looks deeper than the skin of his body, it is a mark of blight. The priest shall look at him and declare him unclean.

4But if the bright spot on the skin of his body is white and does not look deeper than the skin, and its hair has not turned white, the priest shall shut the marked man away for seven days.

5The priest shall look at him on the seventh day. If the mark has stayed as it was and has not spread in the skin, the priest shall shut him away another seven days.

6The priest shall look at him again on the seventh day. If the mark has faded and has not spread in the skin, the priest shall declare him clean. It is a scab. He shall wash his clothes and be clean.

7But if the scab keeps spreading in the skin after he has shown himself to the priest for his cleansing, he shall show himself to the priest a second time.

8The priest shall look. If the scab has spread in the skin, the priest shall declare him unclean. It is blight.

When It Covers Everything

9When a mark of blight is on a person, he shall be brought to the priest.

10The priest shall look. If there is a white swelling in the skin and it has turned the hair white, and there is raw flesh in the swelling,

11it is an old blight in the skin of his body, and the priest shall declare him unclean. The priest shall not shut him away, because he is unclean.

12But if the blight breaks out all over the skin, and covers all the skin of the marked man from his head to his feet, everywhere the priest can see,

13then the priest shall look. If the blight has covered all his flesh, he shall declare the marked man clean. It has all turned white; he is clean.

14But on the day raw flesh appears on him he shall be unclean.

15The priest shall look at the raw flesh and declare him unclean. The raw flesh is unclean; it is blight.

16But if the raw flesh changes back and turns white, he shall come to the priest,

17and the priest shall look at him. If the mark has turned white, the priest shall declare the marked man clean. He is clean.

A Boil and a Burn

18When there is a boil on the skin of someone's body and it heals,

19and in the place of the boil there is a white swelling or a reddish-white bright spot, it shall be shown to the priest.

20The priest shall look. If it looks lower than the skin and its hair has turned white, the priest shall declare him unclean. It is a mark of blight that has broken out in the boil.

21But if the priest looks at it and there is no white hair in it, and it is not lower than the skin, and it is faded, then the priest shall shut him away seven days.

22If it keeps spreading in the skin, the priest shall declare him unclean. It is a mark.

23But if the bright spot stays where it is and has not spread, it is the scar of the boil, and the priest shall declare him clean.

24Or when someone has a burn on the skin of his body, and the raw place of the burn becomes a reddish-white or white bright spot,

25the priest shall look at it. If the hair in the bright spot has turned white and it looks deeper than the skin, it is blight that has broken out in the burn. The priest shall declare him unclean. It is a mark of blight.

26But if the priest looks at it and there is no white hair in the bright spot, and it is not lower than the skin, and it is faded, then the priest shall shut him away seven days.

27The priest shall look at him on the seventh day. If it keeps spreading in the skin, the priest shall declare him unclean. It is a mark of blight.

28But if the bright spot stays where it is and has not spread in the skin, and it is faded, it is the swelling of the burn, and the priest shall declare him clean, because it is the scar of the burn.

On the Head or in the Beard

29When a man or a woman has a mark on the head or in the beard,

30the priest shall look at the mark. If it looks deeper than the skin and there is thin yellow hair in it, the priest shall declare him unclean. It is a scaly patch; it is blight of the head or of the beard.

31When the priest looks at the mark of the scaly patch and it does not look deeper than the skin, and there is no black hair in it, then the priest shall shut the marked person away for seven days.

32The priest shall look at the mark on the seventh day. If the scaly patch has not spread, and there is no yellow hair in it, and the patch does not look deeper than the skin,

33then he shall shave himself, but he shall not shave the patch; and the priest shall shut him away another seven days.

34The priest shall look at the scaly patch on the seventh day. If the patch has not spread in the skin and does not look deeper than the skin, the priest shall declare him clean. He shall wash his clothes and be clean.

35But if the scaly patch keeps spreading in the skin after he has been declared clean,

36the priest shall look at him. If the patch has spread in the skin, the priest does not need to look for the yellow hair. He is unclean.

37But if the patch has stayed as it was and black hair has grown in it, the patch is healed. He is clean, and the priest shall declare him clean.

What Is Not a Mark

38When a man or a woman has bright spots on the skin of the body, white bright spots,

39the priest shall look. If the bright spots on the skin of their body are a faded white, it is a rash that has broken out in the skin. He is clean.

40When a man's head loses its hair, he is bald. He is clean.

41If he loses the hair at the front of his head, he is bald at the forehead. He is clean.

42But if there is a reddish-white mark on the bald head or the bald forehead, it is blight breaking out on his bald head or his bald forehead.

43The priest shall look at him. If the swelling of the mark is reddish-white on his bald head or his bald forehead, looking like blight on the skin of the body,

44he is a blighted man. He is unclean. The priest shall certainly declare him unclean; his mark is on his head.

Outside the Camp

45The person who has the blight, who has the mark on him — his clothes shall be torn and his hair shall hang loose, and he shall cover his upper lip and call out, "Unclean! Unclean!"

46All the days the mark is on him he shall be unclean. He is unclean. He shall live alone; his home shall be outside the camp.

On Cloth and on Leather

47When a garment has a mark of blight on it, whether a wool garment or a linen garment,

48or on the warp or the weft of the linen or the wool, or on leather or on anything made of leather,

49and the mark is greenish or reddish in the garment, or on the leather, or on the warp or the weft, or on any leather object, it is a mark of blight, and it shall be shown to the priest.

50The priest shall look at the mark and shut the marked thing away for seven days.

51He shall look at the mark on the seventh day. If the mark has spread in the garment, or in the warp or the weft, or in the leather, whatever the leather is used for, the mark is a malignant blight. It is unclean.

52He shall burn the garment, or the warp or the weft, in wool or in linen, or any leather object that has the mark on it, because it is a malignant blight. It shall be burned in the fire.

53But if the priest looks and the mark has not spread in the garment, or in the warp or the weft, or in any leather object,

54then the priest shall order that the thing with the mark on it be washed, and he shall shut it away another seven days.

55The priest shall look after the mark has been washed. If the mark has not changed its look, and the mark has not spread, it is unclean. You shall burn it in the fire. It is an eaten-through spot, whether on the back of it or on the front.

56But if the priest looks and the mark has faded after it was washed, then he shall tear it out of the garment, or out of the leather, or out of the warp or the weft.

57If it appears again in the garment, or in the warp or the weft, or in any leather object, it is breaking out. You shall burn in the fire whatever has the mark on it.

58If you wash the garment, or the warp or the weft, or any leather object, and the mark leaves it, it shall be washed a second time, and it will be clean.

59This is the instruction for a mark of blight in a garment of wool or linen, or in the warp or the weft, or in any leather object, to declare it clean or to declare it unclean.

Notes

  • v2 "blight" — tsara'at, and it is not leprosy. English Bibles have printed leprosy since the Greek translators reached for lepra, a general word for scaly skin, and Latin and then English took it from them. Read what the chapter actually legislates for: a condition that turns hair white; that can cover a body completely, at which point the person is declared clean (v13); that breaks out in wool, in linen, in leather (vv47–59) and, in the next chapter, in the plaster of a house. No single illness does all of that. At Exodus 4:6 it arrives on Moses' hand and leaves again inside two verses. What the word names is not a diagnosis but a spreading ruin in a surface — skin, cloth, or wall — and the priest's whole job is to decide whether it is spreading.

  • v2 "a mark" — nega, from naga, to touch. The noun is a touch, a stroke — the same verb that ran through chapter 11, where anyone who touches a carcass is unclean until evening. What is on the skin is described as something that has touched the person, not something they have. The chapter uses it forty-seven times.

  • the priest is not a physician — he prescribes nothing. In fifty-nine verses there is no treatment, no ointment, no prayer, no cure. He looks, he waits seven days, he looks again, and he says one of two words: clean or unclean. Nothing here is about making anyone better. It is about deciding what may come near.

  • vv12–13 covered head to foot, and clean — the verse that rules out any reading of this as a contagion law. A man whose skin is entirely white is sent home; a man with one patch of raw flesh is put out (v14). Whatever the priest is looking for, more of it is not worse. The dangerous state is the one in flux — something spreading, something changing — and the moment it stops changing the man is clean, however he looks.

  • v4 "shall shut the marked man away" — hisgir, to close in, and this is the first quarantine in literature that gets a written procedure: seven days, look, seven days again, look. It is not punishment and it is not treatment. It is time, used as an instrument — the law's way of asking a question that only waiting can answer.

  • v30 "a scaly patch" — netek, from a verb meaning to tear or pull away, used of a hair coming out and of a cord snapping. On the head and in the beard the test changes: not white hair but thin yellow hair, and v33 requires the man to shave around the patch and leave the patch itself unshaved, so the priest can see whether its edge has moved. The procedure is designed for a second look a week later.

  • v39 the look-alike that is clean — bohaq, some faded white patchiness of the skin, and the law names it in order to let it go. Two verses later baldness gets the same treatment twice over (vv40–41): he is bald. He is clean. A chapter this severe about what to exclude takes the trouble to say out loud which ordinary things are not it.

  • v45 "Unclean! Unclean!" — the man is made to announce himself. And the two things he must do — torn clothes and loose hair — are the two things Aaron was forbidden at 10:6, in the same words, paro'a and parom. What the high priest may not do in the worst grief of his life is imposed on this man as a permanent condition. He is dressed as a mourner, and the person he is mourning is himself.

  • v46 "He shall live alone" — badad yeshev. Lamentations opens with the same two words turned on a city: How lonely sits the city that was full of people — yashvah vadad ha-ir. The phrase belongs to this law first, and the poet later says of Jerusalem what the law says of one man with a mark on his skin.

  • vv47–59 the same word, on a coat — the section that makes leprosy impossible. A garment gets tsara'at; so do the warp and the weft, and a leather bag; and the procedure is identical to the one for a human being, down to the two seven-day waits. What the cloth gets is called tsara'at mam'eret, a malignant blight, a word used three times in the Bible — twice here and once in chapter 14, of a house.

  • v55 "an eaten-through spot" — pechetet, which occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, in this verse, and is related to a word for a pit or hollow. The sense is that something has gone through the fabric. It is the last technical term the chapter introduces and there is nothing to check it against.

  • what the chapter never says — no cause is given, anywhere. Not sin, not contact, not punishment, not uncleanness caught from someone else. The narratives elsewhere do link it to a person's conduct — Miriam at Numbers 12:10, Uzziah at 2 Chronicles 26:19 — but the law itself is silent, and reading those stories back into it turns a procedure for looking at skin into a verdict on the person, which is the one thing these fifty-nine verses refuse to do.

chapters.title: Coming Back In
chapters.html:
Leviticus 14

Outside the Camp, and the Two Birds

1The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,

2"This shall be the instruction for the person with the blight on the day of his cleansing. He shall be brought to the priest,

3and the priest shall go outside the camp. The priest shall look. If the mark of blight has healed in the blighted man,

4the priest shall order that two live clean birds be taken for the one being cleansed, with cedar wood, scarlet yarn and hyssop.

5The priest shall order that one of the birds be slaughtered into a clay pot, over fresh running water.

6He shall take the live bird with the cedar wood, the scarlet yarn and the hyssop, and dip them all in the blood of the bird slaughtered over the fresh running water,

7and sprinkle it seven times on the one being cleansed from the blight, and declare him clean; and he shall let the live bird go free over the open field.

8The one being cleansed shall wash his clothes and shave off all his hair and bathe in water, and he is clean. After that he may come into the camp — but he shall stay outside his tent for seven days.

9On the seventh day he shall shave off all his hair — his head, his beard and his eyebrows, every hair. He shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and he is clean.

The Eighth Day

10On the eighth day he shall take two unblemished male lambs, and one unblemished ewe lamb a year old, and three tenths of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering, and one log of oil.

11The priest who does the cleansing shall set the man being cleansed, and these things, before the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting.

12The priest shall take one of the lambs and present it as a guilt offering, with the log of oil, and wave them before the LORD.

13He shall slaughter the lamb in the place where the sin offering and the burnt offering are slaughtered, in the holy place — because the guilt offering, like the sin offering, belongs to the priest. It is most holy.

14The priest shall take some of the blood of the guilt offering and put it on the lobe of the right ear of the one being cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot.

15The priest shall take some of the log of oil and pour it into his own left palm,

16and dip his right finger in the oil on his left palm and sprinkle some of it with his finger seven times before the LORD.

17From the oil left in his palm the priest shall put some on the lobe of the right ear of the one being cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot — on top of the blood of the guilt offering.

18He shall put what is left of the oil in his palm on the head of the one being cleansed, and the priest shall make atonement for him before the LORD.

19The priest shall offer the sin offering and make atonement for the one being cleansed from his uncleanness, and after that he shall slaughter the burnt offering.

20The priest shall offer up the burnt offering and the grain offering on the altar, and make atonement for him, and he is clean.

If He Cannot Afford It

21If he is poor and cannot afford so much, he shall take one lamb as a guilt offering to be waved, to make atonement for him, and one tenth of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering, and a log of oil,

22and two turtledoves or two young pigeons, whichever he can afford — one shall be a sin offering and the other a burnt offering.

23On the eighth day he shall bring them for his cleansing to the priest, to the entrance of the tent of meeting, before the LORD.

24The priest shall take the lamb of the guilt offering and the log of oil, and wave them before the LORD.

25He shall slaughter the lamb of the guilt offering, and the priest shall take some of the blood of the guilt offering and put it on the lobe of the right ear of the one being cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot.

26The priest shall pour some of the oil into his own left palm,

27and with his right finger sprinkle some of the oil in his left palm seven times before the LORD.

28From the oil in his palm the priest shall put some on the lobe of the right ear of the one being cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot — on the place where the blood of the guilt offering was.

29He shall put what is left of the oil in his palm on the head of the one being cleansed, to make atonement for him before the LORD.

30He shall offer the turtledoves or the young pigeons, whichever he can afford —

31one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering, with the grain offering. The priest shall make atonement for the one being cleansed, before the LORD.

32This is the instruction for the person who has a mark of blight, who cannot afford the full offering for his cleansing."

Blight in a House

33The LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying,

34"When you come into the land of Canaan, which I am giving you as a holding, and I put a mark of blight in a house in the land you hold,

35the owner of the house shall come and tell the priest, 'Something like a mark has appeared in my house.'

36The priest shall order the house emptied before he goes in to look at the mark, so that nothing in the house becomes unclean. After that the priest shall go in to look at the house.

37He shall look at the mark. If the mark is in the walls of the house, in greenish or reddish hollows that look lower than the wall,

38the priest shall go out of the house to its doorway and shut it up for seven days.

39The priest shall come back on the seventh day and look. If the mark has spread in the walls of the house,

40the priest shall order that the stones with the mark in them be pulled out and thrown outside the city, to an unclean place.

41He shall have the house scraped all around inside, and they shall pour out the plaster they scraped off outside the city, to an unclean place.

42They shall take other stones and put them in place of the old ones, and he shall take fresh plaster and replaster the house.

43If the mark comes back and breaks out in the house after the stones have been pulled out, and after the house has been scraped and plastered,

44the priest shall come and look. If the mark has spread in the house, it is a malignant blight in the house. It is unclean.

45He shall tear down the house — its stones and its timbers and all the plaster of the house — and carry it outside the city, to an unclean place.

46Anyone who goes into the house during all the days it is shut up shall be unclean until evening.

47Anyone who sleeps in the house shall wash his clothes, and anyone who eats in the house shall wash his clothes.

48But if the priest comes and looks, and the mark has not spread in the house after the house was plastered, then the priest shall declare the house clean, because the mark has healed.

49To purify the house he shall take two birds, and cedar wood, and scarlet yarn, and hyssop.

50He shall slaughter one of the birds into a clay pot, over fresh running water,

51and take the cedar wood and the hyssop and the scarlet yarn and the live bird, and dip them in the blood of the slaughtered bird and in the fresh running water, and sprinkle the house seven times.

52He shall purify the house with the blood of the bird and with the fresh running water and with the live bird and with the cedar wood and with the hyssop and with the scarlet yarn.

53He shall let the live bird go free outside the city, over the open field, and make atonement for the house; and it is clean.

This Is the Instruction

54This is the instruction for every mark of blight, and for a scaly patch,

55and for blight in a garment and in a house,

56and for a swelling and a scab and a bright spot,

57to teach when something is unclean and when it is clean. This is the instruction for blight.

Notes

  • v3 "the priest shall go outside the camp" — the man cannot come to the sanctuary, so the priest walks out to him. It is the only time in these chapters that the priesthood leaves its own ground to meet somebody, and it happens at the start of a ceremony that will end with that man standing at the entrance of the tent. The whole chapter is the distance of that walk being closed from both ends.

  • vv4–7 the two birds — the first is killed into a clay pot held over fresh running water; the second is dipped in its blood and released over open country. Nothing is burned, nothing is eaten, nothing goes on the altar, and the whole thing happens outside the camp before the man is clean. It is not a sacrifice. The nearest thing to it in the Torah is the goat of chapter 16, sent away alive into the wilderness — and the verb is the same, shillach, to send off. One living creature carries something away and is not killed.

  • v4 cedar, scarlet, hyssop — the same three appear together at Numbers 19:6, thrown into the fire under the red heifer. Hyssop by itself is the brush that put blood on the doorposts at the Passover (Exodus 12:22) and the word David reaches for in Psalm 51:7, purge me with hyssop and I shall be clean. It is a small rough plant that holds liquid well. The cedar is the opposite — the largest timber in the region — and the text pairs them without comment.

  • v5 "fresh running water" — mayim chayyim, literally living water: water that moves, from a spring or a stream, as against water standing in a jar. The phrase is ordinary Hebrew for running water and becomes something else entirely in the prophets, where God is the fountain of living water that Israel abandoned (Jeremiah 2:13). Here it is a practical instruction about which bucket to use.

  • v14 the ear, the thumb, the toe — this is the rite of 8:23, where Moses put blood on Aaron's right ear, right thumb and right big toe to make him a priest. The gesture occurs in the Hebrew Bible in these two ceremonies and nowhere else. The man being brought back in from outside the camp is handled with the ritual that installs a high priest — and then, in vv15–18, he is anointed with oil as well, oil on top of the blood, and the last of it poured on his head. Aaron was anointed on the head too (8:12).

  • v12 a guilt offering, for a man who was ill — the offering of chapter 5, brought for breach of faith and for defrauding a neighbor, is required here from someone whose only recorded act is having had a mark on his skin. No wrong is named. As at 12:6, the name of an offering turns out not to be a statement about what the person did.

  • v10 "one log of oil" — log, a liquid measure, and the chapter never says how much it is. It is mentioned five times in these verses and the text is more interested in which palm the priest pours it into than in the quantity.

  • vv15–18 the left hand — the priest pours the oil into his own left palm and dips his right finger into it. The detail is given twice, in both the full rite and the cheaper one, and it is the only place in Leviticus where the two hands are told apart. Everything else in the chapter that specifies a side specifies the right.

  • v21 "cannot afford so much" — ein yado masseget, from nasag, to overtake or catch up to. This is the third idiom Leviticus uses for the same thing, and all three are about the hand rather than about money: his hand does not reach (5:7), her hand does not find (12:8), and now his hand does not overtake. Three different verbs, one gesture — someone stretching for something just out of range.

  • v34 "and I put a mark of blight in a house" — the only place in these two chapters where a cause is given for any of this, and the cause is God, speaking in the first person, about houses that do not exist yet in a land they have not entered. The sentence sits in the middle of a procedure manual: the same paragraph that explains how to scrape plaster says who puts the blight in the wall. Chapter 13 refused to say where a mark on skin comes from. This one verse says, of walls only, that it comes from Him.

  • v36 "order the house emptied" — before the priest goes in, because the moment he says the word everything under that roof is unclean. The law is arranged so that a man does not lose his furniture along with his house. It is a small mercy written into a procedure that may end with the building pulled down, and it works only because uncleanness here begins with the priest's verdict rather than with the mark.

  • v37 "hollows" — sheqa'arurot, a word that occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, in this verse. It is built on a root for sinking or being depressed, and it is describing what the priest sees: greenish or reddish patches that look lower than the surface of the wall. The rest of the sentence carries the sense even though the word itself has nothing to check it against.

  • v45 "he shall tear down the house" — and this is where the chapter's vocabulary arrives somewhere unexpected. A person with the blight is put outside the camp and waited on until he heals; a house that does not stop spreading is demolished and carted off in pieces. The procedures are identical up to the last step, and then the one for the building has no mercy in it at all.

chapters.title: What the Body Gives Off
chapters.html:
Leviticus 15

A Man with a Discharge

1The LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying,

2"Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: When any man has a discharge from his body, his discharge is unclean.

3This is how his discharge makes him unclean: whether his body runs with it or is stopped up by it, he is unclean.

4Every bed the man with the discharge lies on is unclean, and everything he sits on is unclean.

5Anyone who touches his bed shall wash his clothes and bathe in water, and be unclean until evening.

6Whoever sits on anything the man with the discharge sat on shall wash his clothes and bathe in water, and be unclean until evening.

7Whoever touches the body of the man with the discharge shall wash his clothes and bathe in water, and be unclean until evening.

8If the man with the discharge spits on someone who is clean, that person shall wash his clothes and bathe in water, and be unclean until evening.

9Anything he rides on is unclean.

10Anyone who touches anything that was under him shall be unclean until evening; and whoever carries those things shall wash his clothes and bathe in water, and be unclean until evening.

11If the man with the discharge touches anyone without first rinsing his hands in water, that person shall wash his clothes and bathe in water, and be unclean until evening.

12A clay pot that the man with the discharge touches shall be broken, and every wooden vessel shall be rinsed in water.

13When the man with the discharge becomes clean of his discharge, he shall count seven days for his cleansing, and wash his clothes and bathe his body in fresh running water, and he is clean.

14On the eighth day he shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons and come before the LORD, to the entrance of the tent of meeting, and give them to the priest.

15The priest shall offer them, one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering, and make atonement for him before the LORD for his discharge.

Emissions

16When a man has an emission of semen, he shall bathe his whole body in water, and be unclean until evening.

17Every garment and every hide with semen on it shall be washed in water, and be unclean until evening.

18When a man lies with a woman and has an emission of semen, they shall both bathe in water, and be unclean until evening.

A Woman's Flow

19When a woman has a discharge, and the discharge in her body is blood, she shall be in her monthly separation seven days, and anyone who touches her shall be unclean until evening.

20Everything she lies on in her separation is unclean, and everything she sits on is unclean.

21Anyone who touches her bed shall wash his clothes and bathe in water, and be unclean until evening.

22Anyone who touches anything she sits on shall wash his clothes and bathe in water, and be unclean until evening.

23If anything is on her bed or on whatever she is sitting on, whoever touches it shall be unclean until evening.

24If a man lies with her and her separation comes on him, he shall be unclean seven days, and every bed he lies on shall be unclean.

A Flow Out of Season

25When a woman's flow of blood runs many days at a time that is not her monthly separation, or when it runs past her separation, all the days of her unclean flow she shall be as in the days of her separation. She is unclean.

26Every bed she lies on all the days of her flow shall be to her like the bed of her separation, and everything she sits on shall be unclean, like the uncleanness of her separation.

27Anyone who touches these things shall be unclean, and shall wash his clothes and bathe in water, and be unclean until evening.

28When she becomes clean of her flow, she shall count seven days for herself, and after that she is clean.

29On the eighth day she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons and bring them to the priest, to the entrance of the tent of meeting.

30The priest shall offer one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering, and make atonement for her before the LORD for her unclean flow.

Why This Matters

31You shall keep the sons of Israel separate from their uncleanness, so that they do not die in their uncleanness by defiling My dwelling, which is among them."

32This is the instruction for the man with a discharge, and for the man who has an emission of semen and is unclean by it,

33and for the woman who is unwell in her separation, and for anyone with a discharge, male or female, and for a man who lies with an unclean woman.

Notes

  • v2 "a discharge" — zav, from zuv, to flow, and it is the same verb as the most famous promise in the Torah. The land Israel is being taken to is zavat chalav u-dvash, flowing with milk and honey (Exodus 3:8). One root covers the abundance of the promised land and the thing a man's body does that puts him outside the camp. Hebrew does not hear two words there; it hears one, used of anything that will not stop coming out.

  • v2 "from his body" — mi-besaro, literally from his flesh, and here it is a euphemism: the chapter is about the genitals and says so by not saying so. The same word is used plainly for flesh two verses later. This rendering keeps the Hebrew's own indirection rather than replacing it with clinical language the text declined to use.

  • v3 the hard verse — rar besaro et zovo o hechtim besaro mi-zovo. Rar is a word for running or slavering; hechtim is built on chatam, to seal up. So the sentence covers the condition whether the flow is running or blocked, which is medically sensible and grammatically strange, and neither verb occurs often enough to be pinned down. The verse is left rough here because it is rough.

  • uncleanness is not sin — the distinction the whole chapter depends on, and the one most likely to be misread. Nothing described here is a wrong. Nobody is blamed, nobody is punished, and two of the causes are ordinary marital relations (v18) and a woman's monthly cycle (v19). The remedy is water and sunset. Tamei is a status, like being wet — it says where a person may go, not what kind of person they are — and the only reason it matters at all is given in v31.

  • v18 both of them, and nothing else — a couple who have slept together wash and wait until evening. That is the entire law. No offering, no confession, no priest, and no suggestion that anything wrong happened. The verse is remarkable mostly for what it does not contain, given how much later writing has been built on it.

  • v19 "her monthly separation" — niddah, from a root meaning to move away or be put aside. It names the state, not the woman, and the chapter treats it in exactly the same words it used for the man in vv4–12: beds, seats, whoever touches them, wash, wait. The symmetry is deliberate and runs for thirty verses — one flow for a man, one for a woman, the same procedures, the same two birds at the end.

  • vv24 and 20:18 do not agree — here, a man who lies with a woman in her separation is unclean for seven days, the same as the bed he slept on. At 20:18 the same act ends with both of them cut off from among their people. Two penalties for one action, in one book, and neither passage mentions the other. It is the kind of seam the Torah leaves visible, and no note can close it honestly.

  • v25 the woman whose flow does not stop — a chronic condition, treated at length and with no stigma attached beyond the same rules that apply to everyone else in the chapter. This is the law the woman in the crowd at Mark 5:25 has been living under: the Greek says she was in a flow of blood twelve years, using the word the Greek Old Testament uses for zov. What she then does is reach through a crowd and take hold of a man's cloak (5:27) — and by vv21–27 here, touching is exactly what transmits. In Mark the transmission runs the other way.

  • v31 the reason, finally — thirty verses of beds and seats and washing, and then the point: so that they do not die in their uncleanness by defiling My dwelling, which is among them. The rules are not about hygiene and not about morality. They exist because of where God has chosen to live. Mishkani, My dwelling, is the word from Exodus 25:9, and the last three words of the verse are the whole problem — asher be-tokham, which is among them. Something holy has been set down in the middle of an ordinary camp full of bodies, and the rest follows from that.

This is the instruction for the man with a discharge, and for the man who has an emission of semen and is unclean by it,
and for the woman who is unwell in her separation, and for anyone with a discharge, male or female, and for a man who lies with an unclean woman.

chapters.title: Once a Year
chapters.html:
Leviticus 16

After the Death of the Two Sons

1The LORD spoke to Moses after the death of Aaron's two sons, when they came near before the LORD and died.

2The LORD said to Moses, "Tell Aaron your brother that he must not come at just any time into the holy place inside the veil, in front of the cover on the ark, or he will die — because I appear in the cloud over the cover.

3This is how Aaron shall come into the holy place: with a young bull for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering.

4He shall put on a holy linen tunic, and linen undergarments shall be on his body, and he shall tie a linen sash around him and wind a linen turban on his head. These are holy garments. He shall bathe his body in water and put them on.

5From the congregation of the sons of Israel he shall take two male goats for a sin offering and one ram for a burnt offering.

The Two Goats

6Aaron shall present his own bull for the sin offering and make atonement for himself and for his household.

7He shall take the two goats and set them before the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting.

8Aaron shall cast lots over the two goats: one lot for the LORD and one lot for Azazel.

9Aaron shall present the goat on which the lot for the LORD fell, and offer it as a sin offering.

10The goat on which the lot for Azazel fell shall be set alive before the LORD, to make atonement over it, to send it away to Azazel into the wilderness.

Inside the Veil

11Aaron shall present his own bull for the sin offering and make atonement for himself and for his household; he shall slaughter his own bull for the sin offering.

12He shall take a fire pan full of burning coals from the altar before the LORD, and two handfuls of finely ground fragrant incense, and bring them inside the veil.

13He shall put the incense on the fire before the LORD, and the cloud of the incense shall hide the cover that is over the Testimony, so that he does not die.

14He shall take some of the blood of the bull and sprinkle it with his finger on the front of the cover, on the east side; and he shall sprinkle some of the blood seven times with his finger in front of the cover.

15He shall slaughter the people's goat for the sin offering and bring its blood inside the veil, and do with its blood as he did with the blood of the bull, and sprinkle it on the cover and in front of the cover.

16He shall make atonement for the holy place because of the uncleanness of the sons of Israel and because of their rebellions, for all their sins. So he shall do for the tent of meeting, which dwells with them in the middle of their uncleanness.

17No one at all shall be in the tent of meeting when he goes in to make atonement in the holy place, until he comes out. He shall make atonement for himself and for his household and for the whole assembly of Israel.

18He shall go out to the altar that is before the LORD and make atonement for it, and take some of the blood of the bull and some of the blood of the goat and put it on the horns of the altar all around.

19He shall sprinkle some of the blood on it with his finger seven times, and cleanse it from the uncleanness of the sons of Israel and set it apart.

The Goat That Goes Away

20When he has finished making atonement for the holy place and the tent of meeting and the altar, he shall present the live goat.

21Aaron shall lean both his hands on the head of the live goat and confess over it all the guilt of the sons of Israel and all their rebellions, for all their sins, and put them on the head of the goat, and send it away into the wilderness by the hand of a man appointed for it.

22The goat shall carry on itself all their guilt to a land cut off; and he shall send the goat away in the wilderness.

23Aaron shall come into the tent of meeting and take off the linen garments he put on when he went into the holy place, and leave them there.

24He shall bathe his body in water in a holy place and put on his garments, and come out and offer his burnt offering and the people's burnt offering, and make atonement for himself and for the people.

25He shall turn the fat of the sin offering into smoke on the altar.

26The one who sends the goat away to Azazel shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and after that he may come into the camp.

27The bull of the sin offering and the goat of the sin offering, whose blood was brought in to make atonement in the holy place, shall be carried outside the camp, and their hides and their flesh and their dung shall be burned in the fire.

28The one who burns them shall wash his clothes and bathe his body in water, and after that he may come into the camp.

Once a Year

29This shall be a lasting statute for you: in the seventh month, on the tenth of the month, you shall afflict yourselves and do no work at all — neither the native nor the guest living among you —

30because on this day atonement shall be made for you, to cleanse you. You shall be clean before the LORD from all your sins.

31It is a sabbath of complete rest for you, and you shall afflict yourselves. It is a lasting statute.

32The priest who is anointed and whose hand is filled to serve as priest in place of his father shall make the atonement, and he shall put on the linen garments, the holy garments,

33and make atonement for the most holy place, for the tent of meeting and for the altar; and he shall make atonement for the priests and for all the people of the assembly.

34This shall be a lasting statute for you, to make atonement for the sons of Israel for all their sins once a year." He did as the LORD commanded Moses.

Notes

  • v1 where this chapter is anchored — the greatest day in Israel's calendar is dated, in its first sentence, by a funeral. After the death of Aaron's two sons, when they came near before the LORD and died. Chapter 10 left that event without an explanation and Aaron without an answer. What arrives six chapters later is not an explanation but a procedure: this is how a man goes in there and comes out alive.

  • v4 the clothes he does not wear — Exodus 28 spends a chapter on gold, blue, purple, crimson, the breastpiece with twelve stones, the golden plate reading Holy to the LORD. On the one day of the year the high priest enters the innermost room, he takes all of it off and dresses in plain linen — tunic, undergarments, sash, turban, nothing else. The text still calls them holy garments. He goes in looking like nobody.

  • v8 "Azazel" — la-azazel, and nobody knows what it means. The word occurs four times in the Hebrew Bible, all of them in this chapter, and nowhere else. Three readings have been argued for centuries: that it is a compound of ez, goat, and azal, to go away — the source of English scapegoat, coined by Tyndale; that it is an abstract noun meaning utter removal; or that it is a name. The grammar of this verse leans to the third, because of the parallel it sets up — one lot for the LORD and one lot for Azazel — where the matching term is a person. The text says no more than that, and neither can anyone else.

  • vv8–10 what the lot decides — two goats, identical, bought by the same congregation for the same purpose. One is killed and its blood carried into the holiest room in the world; the other is stood up alive, loaded, and walked out into the desert. Nothing about either animal chooses which. A lot is cast, and that is the whole of the difference between them.

  • v13 the cloud he hides behind — v2 says God appears in the cloud over the cover, and v13 has the high priest raise a cloud of incense to hide that same cover, so that he does not die. The smoke is not decoration and not atmosphere; it is a screen. The one man permitted into the room goes in and immediately obscures his own view of it.

  • v16 "which dwells with them in the middle of their uncleanness" — this is what the last six chapters were building toward. The tent is not a clean place set apart from a dirty camp; it is a holy thing sitting in the middle of ordinary human mess, and 15:31 already said the risk that creates. The atonement in this chapter is made for the building before it is made for anybody in it. The sanctuary itself needs cleaning, and what has dirtied it is everyone living around it.

  • v17 "no one at all" — ve-khol adam lo yihyeh, and adam is the whole human race. Not an assistant, not another priest. For the length of this rite the most populous building in the camp holds one man, and the text pauses to say so.

  • v21 "confess over it" — hitvaddah, from yadah, the verb that first appeared at 5:5 where an ordinary Israelite had to say out loud what he had done, and which also gives the thanksgiving offering its name at 7:12. Here it reaches its largest form: one man, hands on a goat's head, saying the wrongs of an entire nation aloud. The words are not recorded.

  • v21 "both his hands" — the written consonants say his hand, singular; the reading tradition says his hands. Leviticus has five such places, and the other one where Aaron's hand is at issue is 9:22, where he lifts it to bless the people. Both are his hands on or toward Israel, and in both the tradition reads two where the letters say one. Note also that everywhere else in Leviticus one hand is leaned on an animal's head (1:4, 4:4). This is the only sacrifice that takes both.

  • v22 "a land cut off" — erets gezerah, from gazar, to cut. The noun turns up otherwise only in Ezekiel's temple plan, where it names a separated area. So the goat goes to a cut-off land, which is what the wilderness is, and the phrase occurs once in this sense. The animal is not killed and is not an offering. It is transport.

  • vv7, 10, 21–22 and 14:7 — two chapters ago a man returning from outside the camp had two birds taken: one killed over running water, one dipped in its blood and released into open country. Here it is two goats: one killed, one released into the wilderness. The same verb carries both, shillach, to send off, and the same logic — something dies, and something else walks away carrying what was wrong, and is never mentioned again.

  • v29 "you shall afflict yourselves" — te'annu et nafshoteikhem, you shall afflict your souls, and nefesh is the throat and the appetite as much as the inner life. The Torah does not use the word fast here or anywhere in this chapter. What is commanded is a day of doing without, undefined, and the tradition that made it a fast had to read the definition out of this phrase. What the verse does say plainly is who it binds: the native and the foreigner living among them, in the same clause.

  • v34 "once a year" — achat ba-shanah, the last three words before the chapter closes. Everything else in Leviticus runs daily, or when someone sins, or when a woman gives birth, or when a mark appears. This happens once, on a fixed date, whether or not anything has gone wrong — the only rite in the book scheduled by the calendar rather than by an event.

chapters.title: The Life Is in the Blood
chapters.html:
Leviticus 17

Nowhere Else to Kill It

1The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,

2"Speak to Aaron and to his sons and to all the sons of Israel, and say to them: This is what the LORD has commanded:

3Any man of the house of Israel who slaughters an ox or a sheep or a goat in the camp, or who slaughters it outside the camp,

4and has not brought it to the entrance of the tent of meeting to present it as an offering to the LORD before the dwelling of the LORD — blood shall be counted against that man. He has shed blood, and that man shall be cut off from among his people.

5This is so that the sons of Israel will take the sacrifices they have been making out in the open field and bring them to the LORD, to the entrance of the tent of meeting, to the priest, and offer them as peace offerings to the LORD.

6The priest shall dash the blood against the altar of the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and turn the fat into smoke as a soothing aroma to the LORD.

7They shall no longer offer their sacrifices to the goat-spirits they have been prostituting themselves to. This shall be a lasting statute for them through their generations.

8Say to them: Any man of the house of Israel, or of the guests living among them, who offers up a burnt offering or a sacrifice

9and does not bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting to offer it to the LORD — that man shall be cut off from his people.

The Life Is in the Blood

10Any man of the house of Israel, or of the guests living among them, who eats any blood — I will set My face against the person who eats the blood, and cut that person off from among his people.

11For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your lives; for it is the blood that makes atonement by the life.

12That is why I have said to the sons of Israel: None of you shall eat blood, and the guest living among you shall not eat blood.

13Any man of the sons of Israel, or of the guests living among them, who hunts and catches an animal or a bird that may be eaten shall pour out its blood and cover it with earth.

14For the life of all flesh — its blood is its life. I said to the sons of Israel: You shall not eat the blood of any flesh, because the life of all flesh is its blood. Anyone who eats it shall be cut off.

15Any person, native or guest, who eats an animal that died on its own or was torn by beasts shall wash his clothes and bathe in water, and be unclean until evening, and then he is clean.

16But if he does not wash them and does not bathe his body, he carries his guilt."

Notes

  • v4 "He has shed blood" — dam shafakh, and it is the language of murder. Genesis 9:6: one who sheds the blood of the human, by the human his blood shall be shed — the same verb with the same noun. A man who butchers his own ox in the wrong place is described in the vocabulary reserved for killing a person. The verb before it is yechashev, shall be counted, the accounting word from 7:18 and from Genesis 15:6: something is entered against his name.

  • v7 "the goat-spirits" — se'irim, hairy ones, the ordinary Hebrew word for he-goats, here plural with the article and clearly meaning something that can be sacrificed to. And it is the same word, in the same form, as the two goats of the previous chapter (16:8). One chapter after the Day of Atonement assigns two se'irim by lot, the next forbids sacrificing to the se'irim. Whatever they are — the word is used again of the creatures that dance in Babylon's ruins at Isaiah 13:21 — the text will not say more about them than that Israel has been going to them.

  • v7 "prostituting themselves to" — zonim achareihem, from zanah, the plain word for prostitution. It is the Bible's standing metaphor for worshipping anything else, and it is not a polite one: the relationship is marriage and the offense is infidelity, not error. Softening it to going astray removes the only thing the sentence is doing.

  • vv3–9 the point of the restriction — an Israelite may not kill an ox anywhere but at the one door. Not because slaughter is wrong, but because sacrifice in the open field is what they have been doing, and to whom. The law does not argue with the practice; it moves it. Everything gets brought to one place where a priest can see it.

  • v11 "the life of the flesh is in the blood" — nefesh ha-basar ba-dam hi, and nefesh is the word English Bibles usually print as soul. It is not a spirit that can leave a body; it is breath, throat, appetite, the living of a living thing — the word used of animals in Genesis 1 before it is ever used of a person. So this sentence is not metaphysics. It is a statement about what blood is: the life itself, in liquid form, which is why it may not be eaten and why it is the one substance that can be put on the altar in place of a life.

  • v11 "makes atonement by the life" — ba-nefesh yekhapper, three words that can be read at least three ways: the blood atones by means of the life in it, or in place of a life, or at the cost of a life. The preposition be carries all three and the verse does not choose. It is the single most quoted sentence in Leviticus and its last clause has never been settled.

  • v13 covering the blood of a hunted animal — a deer or a bird killed out in the hills cannot be brought to the altar, so its blood is poured on the ground and buried. No priest, no altar, nobody watching. The rule reaches the one situation where there is no institution to enforce it, and makes it a matter of what a man does alone on a hillside with a spade.

  • vv8, 10, 12, 13, 15 "the guest" — ger, and the chapter names him in every single paragraph, five times in sixteen verses. The blood law is one of the few in Leviticus that binds the non-Israelite exactly as it binds the native. What is at stake here is not identity; it is the ground everyone is standing on.

  • v10 "I will set My face against" — ve-natatti panai, and God stops speaking through a procedure and speaks in the first person about an individual. Everywhere else the penalty is he shall be cut off, passive, with nobody named as doing the cutting. Here the sentence names Him twice over: I will set My face, and I will cut that person off.
